title: Bring Me the Head of the Machine Gun Woman

facts.text: Director Ernesto Díaz Espinoza shot this gleefully bloody Chilean action-comedy in just 15 days, according to ScreenAnarchy's Fantastic Fest 2012 review.
Cine-vue noted the film opens with grainy, scratched grindhouse film effects, then drops them within minutes, unlike Robert Rodriguez's Planet Terror and Tarantino's Death Proof.
The title nods to Sam Peckinpah's grim 1974 cult film Bring Me the Head of Alfredo Garcia, which also sends a nobody off to fetch a severed head.
For Fantastic Fest 2012, director Ernesto Díaz Espinoza wrote a "drunken review" of his own film after five shots, calling it a LatinXploitation masterpiece filmed in the style of Ed Wood.
Director Ernesto Díaz Espinoza calls his brand of genre filmmaking "LatinXploitation": 70s-style bounty hunter pictures with funky soundtracks and video game culture mixed in.
Star Fernanda Urrejola (Machine Gun Woman) was a Chilean synchronized swimming champion before she became an actress.
GoSeeTalk's Fantastic Fest review says the story is built like a video game quest: DJ Santiago, played by Matías Oviedo, starts at "level 1" in a Chile that plays like the Wild West.
Star Fernanda Urrejola didn't just act: she also helped develop the story with director Ernesto Díaz Espinoza and is credited as co-writer.
The electronic score was composed by Rocco, a regular collaborator of director Ernesto Díaz Espinoza, according to GoSeeTalk's Fantastic Fest 2012 review.
Co-star Jorge Alís (gangster Che Longana) was born in Argentina and now owns a café chantant in Santiago, Chile, called El Cachafaz.
The film premiered September 23, 2012, at Austin's Fantastic Fest. Director Ernesto Díaz Espinoza and star Fernanda Urrejola walked the red carpet and did a Q&A after the first screening.
Ernesto Díaz Espinoza first came to Fantastic Fest in 2007 with Mirageman and Kiltro, the latter billed as the first Chilean martial-arts film, starring his friend Marko Zaror.
Producer Derek Rundell, who also worked on director Ernesto Díaz Espinoza's Kiltro, Mirageman and Mandrill, joined him and star Fernanda Urrejola at Fantastic Fest 2012.
Director Ernesto Díaz Espinoza and martial arts star Marko Zaror have been friends since high school, which is why Zaror headlines so many of the director's films.
Director Ernesto Díaz Espinoza is a big Bud Spencer and Terence Hill fan, and used to give special thanks in his closing credits to the directors who inspired each of his movies.
Rob Simpson of The Geek Show grew tired of the film's repeated driving-scene gag: same music, same camera angle, same blocky GTA-style mission title, by about the sixth or seventh time.
Cast member Daniel Antivilo plays a character called El Tronador. That's also the title of a 2003 mini-DV amateur film Ernesto Díaz Espinoza directed for the Mexploitation market.
Star Matías Oviedo (Santiago) played youth football for Chile's Universidad Católica and later led the long-running Chilean soap Verdades Ocultas.
Cine-vue gave the film two stars out of five, opening with Godard's line that all you need for a movie is a gun and a girl, and suggesting director Ernesto Díaz Espinoza took it too literally.
Rob Simpson of The Geek Show noted the film's violence, mostly squibs and camera tricks, is convincing enough that the movie "doesn't look cheap."
Chile's Radio Universidad de Chile called it "entertainment cinema, aware of its precariousness and its charm," and said the key to enjoying it is not taking it seriously.
The soundtrack includes the cumbia track "Cumbia Sahumerio" by Cholita Sound and "Volteretas" by the group Astro.
Film School Rejects and Complex both named it one of the best films at Austin's Fantastic Fest, and Bloody Disgusting singled out Fernanda Urrejola's performance for praise.
Star Fernanda Urrejola later moved to Los Angeles, appearing in Narcos: Mexico, Clint Eastwood's Cry Macho (2021) and HBO Max's Gossip Girl reboot.
The film reached Chilean theaters on May 23, 2013, eight months after its Fantastic Fest world premiere in Texas.
The Daily Record gave the film three stars, calling it "a fun ride that never outstays its welcome." At roughly 73 minutes, it doesn't.
Matías Oviedo, who plays Santiago, returned to the character's name in 2014's Santiago Violenta, which the film's connections list as a reference to this movie.
Director Ernesto Díaz Espinoza's Mirageman (2007) won over Harry Knowles of Ain't It Cool News, who called it probably one of his favorite superhero movies of all time.
Director Ernesto Díaz Espinoza's earlier film Mandrill (2008) was a suave-assassin riff. This film swaps in a female killer and leaves Marko Zaror out of the lead, per ScreenAnarchy.
